subject: ba
title: International Business Administration
objectives: Define international business and identify why firms choose to go international.
Analyse the political, cultural, legal and economic forces shaping global trade.
Evaluate classical and modern trade theories: Absolute Advantage, Comparative Advantage, and Heckscher-Ohlin.
Understand the mechanics of foreign exchange, tariffs, risk management, and multinational corporations.
study:
International business is the study of transactions across national borders that satisfy the needs of individuals and organisations (Rugman and Collinson). Firms go international to diversify against domestic business-cycle risk, tap growing world markets, respond to foreign competition, access local resources, cut costs, and get around tariff barriers by operating from within a market rather than exporting into it.

Key termExchange Rate — the number of units of one currency needed to purchase one unit of another currency (Morrison, 2006). The foreign exchange market is the 'lubricant' letting companies using different currencies trade without resorting to barter.

Currency deals mostly happen as a spot transaction (immediate exchange, generally settled the second business day) or an outright forward transaction (currency exchanged on a future date at a pre-agreed rate, regardless of where the spot rate actually lands). The US Dollar plays the role of the market's 'vehicle currency.' A tariff is a tax on imported (sometimes exported) goods, used to protect domestic industry, raise government revenue, or serve as a bargaining chip in trade talks.

Classical trade theory starts with Adam Smith's Absolute Cost Advantage: a country should specialise in and export whatever it can produce at a genuinely lower cost than anyone else. David Ricardo went further with Comparative Cost Advantage: a country should specialise based on comparative — not absolute — cost differences, since mutual gains from trade exist even if one country is better at producing everything. J.S. Mill's Reciprocal Demand theory then explains the actual terms of trade (the exchange ratio) between two countries' goods.

Exam tipAbsolute vs comparative advantage is one of the most tested distinctions in this chapter. Absolute = who's better in raw terms; Comparative = who gives up less by specialising (opportunity cost) — the second one is what actually drives beneficial trade.

The modern Heckscher-Ohlin theory explains trade through differences in factor endowments (relative abundance of capital vs labour): a nation exports whatever intensively uses its abundant, cheap factor, and imports whatever needs its scarce, expensive factor. Its companion, the Factor Price Equalisation Theorem, holds that free trade tends to equalise commodity and factor prices across trading countries over time.

International business carries distinct risk categories: political risk (instability, expropriation), economic/financial risk (currency and interest rate swings), legal risk (differing legal systems), operational risk (supply chain disruption), and cultural risk (miscommunication). A Multinational Corporation (MNC) is conventionally defined (Black's Law Dictionary) as a firm deriving 25% or more of its revenue from outside its home country — the East India Company (1600) is cited as one of the earliest examples. MNCs typically evolve through three stages: the Export Stage (starting with export agents), the Foreign Production Stage (choosing between Licensing — low capital and risk, but limited control over the licensee — and Direct Foreign Investment — higher capital and risk, but full control), and finally the Multinational Stage, where production, marketing, R&D and financing are all coordinated globally.
recap:
• Firms go international to diversify risk, access new markets, cut costs, and work around trade barriers.
  • Exchange rate = price of one currency in another; spot (immediate) vs forward (future, pre-agreed rate) transactions; USD is the 'vehicle currency.'
  • Tariff = tax on imports/exports, protecting domestic industry or raising revenue.
  • Absolute Advantage (Smith) = who's outright better; Comparative Advantage (Ricardo) = who has the lower opportunity cost — the real driver of beneficial trade.
  • Heckscher-Ohlin: trade driven by factor endowments (capital vs labour abundance); Factor Price Equalisation: free trade tends to equalise prices across countries over time.
  • Risk types: political, economic/financial, legal, operational, cultural.
  • MNC = 25%+ revenue from abroad; evolves through Export → Foreign Production (Licensing or FDI) → Multinational stages.

quiz.q: According to Rugman and Collinson (2006), international business is best described as:
opts: Only transactions occurring within a single country
A synonym for domestic retail trade
The study of transactions taking place across national borders to satisfy the needs of individuals and organisations
Only government-to-government aid transfers

quiz.q: Which of the following is a reason firms decide to go international, according to Rugman and Collinson (2006)?
opts: To eliminate the need for foreign exchange
To restrict operations strictly to a single city
To diversify against the risks and uncertainties of the domestic business cycle
To avoid any form of competition entirely

quiz.q: An exchange rate, according to Morrison (2006), is defined as:
opts: The number of units of one currency needed to purchase one unit of another currency
The total value of a country's exports
A synonym for a tariff
A fixed tax on all imported goods

quiz.q: The foreign exchange market is described as the 'lubricant' that enables:
opts: Only domestic transactions within one country
Companies in countries using different currencies to trade with each other without resorting to barter
Government tax collection exclusively
The complete elimination of international trade

quiz.q: A Spot Transaction in the foreign exchange market involves:
opts: A transaction that never actually settles
A permanent, irrevocable currency conversion with no settlement date
An exchange of currency scheduled several years into the future with no fixed rate
The immediate exchange of currency, generally settled the second business day after agreement

quiz.q: An Outright Forward Transaction involves:
opts: Only immediate, same-day currency exchange
A transaction limited exclusively to central banks
A transaction with no fixed rate agreed in advance
The exchange of currency on a future date at a pre-agreed forward rate, regardless of the actual spot rate at settlement

quiz.q: The foreign exchange market is characterised by the important role of which currency, described as a 'vehicle currency'?
opts: The US Dollar
The Nigerian Naira exclusively
The Japanese Yen exclusively
Cryptocurrency exclusively

quiz.q: A Tariff is best described as:
opts: A type of insurance policy for exporters
A tax imposed on imported (or sometimes exported) goods to raise their price and protect domestic industry
A form of foreign direct investment
A synonym for a currency swap

quiz.q: According to Adam Smith's Absolute Cost Advantage Theory, a country should:
opts: Avoid all forms of international trade entirely
Focus solely on domestic consumption with no exports
Specialise in and export a commodity in which it has an absolute cost advantage
Import every commodity regardless of cost

quiz.q: David Ricardo's Comparative Cost Advantage Theory holds that trade is determined by:
opts: Government decree alone
Random chance with no economic basis
Only the absolute cost of production, ignoring comparative advantage entirely
Comparative, not absolute, differences in costs between countries

quiz.q: J.S. Mill's theory of Reciprocal Demand primarily helps explain:
opts: The terms of trade (exchange ratio) between two commodities/countries
The total number of firms in a domestic industry
The population growth rate of a nation
The exact location of a country's capital city

quiz.q: The Heckscher-Ohlin theory explains international trade based on differences in:
opts: The size of a country's military
The number of political parties in a country
Factor endowments (relative abundance of capital versus labour) between countries
The colour of national flags

quiz.q: According to the Heckscher-Ohlin theorem, a nation will export the commodity that:
opts: Requires intensive use of the nation's scarce and expensive factor of production
Requires intensive use of the nation's relatively abundant and cheap factor of production
Has no relationship to its factor endowments whatsoever
Is produced using only imported raw materials

quiz.q: The Factor Price Equalisation Theorem suggests that free international trade will:
opts: Have absolutely no effect on prices
Cause permanent, ever-widening price divergence between countries
Only apply to domestic trade, not international trade
Ultimately lead to equalisation of commodity and factor prices across trading countries

quiz.q: New Trade Theories were developed largely because classical and Heckscher-Ohlin theories struggled to explain:
opts: Intra-industry trade between similar developed countries in similar products
The concept of currency exchange rates
The existence of tariffs
Trade between any two countries whatsoever

quiz.q: Which of the following is a risk category identified in international business risk management?
opts: Political Risk, Economic/Financial Risk, and Cultural Risk
Only risks related to domestic retail sales
Only risks related to weather forecasting
Only risks affecting government employees

quiz.q: According to Black's Law Dictionary, a company is considered a multinational corporation if it derives what percentage or more of its revenue from out-of-home-country operations?
Which of the following is cited as one of the first multinational companies, established in 1600?
opts: The World Bank
Nestle
Apple Inc.
The East India Company

quiz.q: In the Export Stage of MNC evolution, firms initially rely on:
opts: Foreign direct manufacturing subsidiaries only
Government-owned trading companies exclusively
Export agents
No form of external assistance whatsoever

quiz.q: In the Foreign Production Stage, Licensing (compared to Direct Foreign Investment) is characterised by:
opts: Complete elimination of any payment to the licensor
Low capital requirement and low risk, but limited managerial control over the licensee
Guaranteed prevention of any rival firm emerging
High capital requirement and full managerial control
